messages.subject: Distance analysis question on nested design.
messages.subject_clean: Distance analysis question on nested design.
messages.body_plain:
I have a rather complex distance analysis that I hope you can be of some
assistance in setting it up for analysis in program Distance.  The project
is a multi species study estimating the density of arboreal rodent nest
structures. There are 5 species of arboreal rodents and the rarer species,
which are the most interesting to us, do not have sufficient detections to
model a detection function using just their detections. Therefore, I was
planning on using all the nests in a global model to estimate the detection
function and than post stratify by species. However our sampling design
also has three strata (conifer stand age\structure classes) in which we
randomly selected a number of conifer stands to sample in each strata. In
each stand we conducted line transect sampling where the lines were laid
out with a random start and within a stand each transect was divided into
2 =96 3 independent segments.

Given Program Distance=92s current limit on analysis of nested designs, I wa=
s
considering using the stand types (3 levels) as a factor covariate and
running an analysis.  What I=92m not sure of is if this is the best approach=

and which options I need to use to obtain the correct standard error
estimates. I would like to have density estimates at both strata level
(each stand type) and at the individual stand level for each species.
Given that all the stands within a stratum were randomly selected from a
larger population of such stands in the study area and that there were
multiple independent transect segments in each stand sampled, I though that
this approach would be statistically valid. However, I=92m not sure how to
set it up.  I also assume that program distance may not be able to
calculate all the estimates and that I may have to calculate part of them
outside the program.  But I=92m not sure of the correct formula.

I would appreciate any advice that you can provide on this analysis.

--

messages.subject: Re: Distance analysis question on nested design.
messages.subject_clean: Distance analysis question on nested design.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian, list,

Let's start by ignoring species, and focus on the analysis for a single
species for which you have enough samples to fit a detection function.  This
means using the data selection part of the data filter in Distance to get
only data for that species.

I'll also assume for now that either (a) within each stratum, all stands are
the same area, or (b) that you selected the random sample of stands within
each stratum with probability proportional to stand area and that within
each selected stand transect line length is proportional to stand area.
Either (a) or (b) mean that you have even coverage probability within
stratum (each point in a stratum has the same probability of being sampled).

For getting estimates of density and standard errors at the stratum level,
and estimates at the stand level, it seems to me you can pool your transects
(someone out there correct me if you disagree).  In this view, the stand is
the random sample for estimating variance in encounter rate.  You simply
pool observations across transects within stands, and make the stand the
"sample" layer in Distance.  You then proceed as normal, fitting detection
functions etc, and estimating density at the stratum and sample (stand)
level.  Note that to get abundance at the stand level, you'll need to
multiply the density estiamtes by the stand area as Distance will only give
you the abundance within the sampled strips at the sample level.

The only thing you can't get out of the above is estimates of the standard
error of density at the stand level, since you've pooled the transects
together.  I might be wrong in reading what you wrote but it seemed to imply
that you only had 2-3 "independent segments" per stand -- in this case you
won't be able to estimate a valid SE at the stand level in any case.

If I'm wrong and you do have lots of independent transects at the stand
level, then you can still do it in Distance, one of two ways:
(1)  If your detection function is global, or you've used stratum as a
covariate then you can still do it in Distance.  Set up a new project in
which stand is the stratum layer, and your transects are at the sample
level.  You'll need your old strata in there as a field if you want to use
them as a covariate.  Then set up the same detection function as previously,
and get a density estimate by stratum layer (i.e., by stand).  This should
be the same as the previous density estiamtes, but now you have a valid SE.
Note that the global density estimate in this case is garbage so ignore it.
(2) If your detection function for this species was by stratum, then you can
set up a similar project to (1), but set up 3 data filters, one for each
stratum (or you could have 3 distance projects).  Then for each stratum, do
an analysis with a global detection function and the density estimate and SE
by "stratum" (i.e., by stand) are what you want.

Now, what about that species for which you had too few detections to model
separately?  A few options here.  The first is to treat the whole question
of whether to estimate a separate detection function for each species, to
use a factor covariate for each species or to pool some or all together just
like any other model selection problem (e.g., what to do about your strata),
and to try all the options and use AIC to guide you.  This assumes you have
no problems in the data that mean that AIC is not reliable.  The usual
bias/variance arguments apply -- although in this case it's most common that
there really are quite large differences in detection function between many
species so the bias can be quite large.  Also, in your case you'll be
constrained in that some species (the rare one) cannot be treated
separately.

If you end up with species as a stratum in the detection function (except
the rare one), you're back with treating each species separately as above.
If species is a covariate, then estimating the appropriate SE for each
species isn't possible analytically using the output that Distance gives
you.  Rather, you'd have to boostrap.  In your example I expect you'd want
to bootstrap by stand and possibly also by transect within stand (assuming
you have enough transects within each stand to do this).  You'd have to
program that bootstrap outside of Distance, calling the MCDS.exe analysis
engine to fit the detection functions -- I've posted on this previously.

So, on balance, you may want to stick to fitting each species separately
apart from the one where you don't have enough data.  For this rare species,
you then need to get a detection function from somewhere -- probably by
bringing in data from a species (or more) that you judge to have similar
detectability.  Note that this obviously means you have to interpret the
density estimates (and CIs) with a pinch of salt.  You can fit the detection
function to the combined data, and then use multipliers to apply this
funciton to only the data from the rare species to get the appropriate
density and SE (see Multipliers in the Distance online manual for how to do
this).  Will work fine for global and by stratum detection functions, but
not for species as a covariate.

OK, so what if you didn't sample in proportion to stand area, or put the
same number of transects in each stand regardless of it's area.  Then you
have less sample coverage in larger stands, and the standard methods in
Distance for computing encounter rate and ER variance won't work.  Also, you
don't have pooling robustness any more (although perheaps it's not that
likely that detection function varies in relation to stand area -- unless
there's a big edge effect).  For calculating density (ie ignoring the
detection function part) there are two issues: one is selection of stands
and the other is coverage of transects within stands.  If you simply took a
random sample of stands and they vary greatly in size and if you think that
density may vary by stand area (e.g., density lower in smaller stands due to
edge effects) you'd better take this into account at the analysis stage.
You can get stratum encounter rate as an weighted mean of the stand
encounter rates, where the weighting is by stand area.  Variance in
encounter rate is then the variance of a weighted mean.  Density can then be
calculated using the standard formulae (Distance book page 76).  If you used
the same sample length in each stand then this is less of a big deal -- you
didn't allocate effort optimally (you usually want effort proportional to
abundance) so may get less efficiency, but the standard Distance analysis I
outlined in the 3rd paragraph, above, can cope with this (bit like visiting
some lines more than once - Distance book page 79).

Sorry for the long answer, but hope it helps,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Truncating data so g(y)=0.15
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jennifer -- I'll post your question and my response to the distance-
sampling list as these are issues that have come up before.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
On Mon, 8 Nov 2004 10:21:20 -0800, Jennifer N Jones wrote:

> >I'm trying to determine an appropriate truncation distance so that
> >g(y)=0.15. All I'm missing is a value for "j" (see below), but can't find
> >an answer in the user's guide, book, or archives. Can you help?

> >Here's what I've done:

> >The distance book recommended using the half-normal key function, which had
> >a reasonable fit. The formula for half-normal is:

> >k(y)=exp[-y2/(2(A1)2]

> >I used cosine for the series expansion, and got a cosine adjustment of
> >order = 2.

> >In the output, the point estimate for parameter  A1 = 13.76, A2 = 0.1651,
> >and f(0) = 0.66939E-01

> >The formula for the cosine series expansion form is (p. 48 distance book,
> >1993):

> >    m
> >sum     ajcos(j pi y/w)
> >    j=2
> >m

> >The formula for calculating probability of detection is:

> >g(y)= key(y)[1+series(y)]/key(0)[1+series(0)]

> >For  half-normal with cosine series expansion , this would be:

> >g(y)= exp[-y2/(2(A1)2][1+ajcos(j pi y/w)]

> >With a 5% truncation, w=27m , and I'll start with y=20m to try to calculate
> >g(y)=.15:

> > g(y)= exp[-202/(2(13.76)2][1+0.1651cos(j pi 20/27)]

> >My question is what is the value for "j"?

> >Thank you for any assistance. I can't move forward with this project until
> >I figure this out!

> >********************************************************
> >Jennifer Jones
> >USDA Forest Service
> >Pacific Southwest Research Station
> >1700 Bayview Dr.
> >Arcata, CA 95521, USA     Tel: (707) 825-2986
> >Email: jnj...@fs.fed.us   Fax: (707) 825-2901
> >**********************************************************
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Answer: In the case of the cosine series, j is the order of the adjustment
term.  The default method in Distance is to start with an adjustment of
order 2, and if that gives lower AIC to try order 3 as well, then order 4,
etc.  For simple and hermite polynomial series, j is the order/2, since it
doesn't make sense to have odd ordered terms.  The default in Distance for
these series is to start with an adjustment of order 4, then try 6, 8 etc.

In your case, you ended up with a cosine term of order 2 in the final model,
so the series expansion is a_2 cos(2 pi y/w).  Therefore

 unscaled g(y)= exp[-y^2/(2(13.76)^2] [1+0.1651cos(2 pi y/27)]

If you're doing this on a calculator, remember that the triganometric
functions are in radians.  One more thing -- you notice I put "unscaled" in
front of g(y).  That's because when there are series expansions, the formula
as given above doesn't give g(0)=1.  So you need:

          g(y) = unscaled g(y)
                 -------------
                 unscaled g(0)

               = exp[-y^2/(2(13.76)^2] [1+0.1651cos(2 pi y/27)]
                 ----------------------------------------------
                 exp[-0^2/(2(13.76)^2] [1+0.1651cos(2 pi 0/27)]

There are some pages about this in the Distance online manual - look in the
index under Detection Function | About Formulae.

The motivation for your question was to find the point at which g(y)=0.15,
to determine a suitable truncation.  Truncation is not an exact science --
for "good" data, it doesn't make much difference whether you truncate at 5%,
10% or g(y) approx. 0.15.  I usually try 5%, try 10% and see if either of
these fits one less adjustment term in some "default" model (hn+cos is
fine), and then just go with that while keeping an eye on the estimated g(w)
and checking it's around 0.15ish (this is for line transects).  I often
round to some convenient whole number (while being aware of any rounding in
the data).  I prefer less truncation to more, all other things being equal.
However, there are lots of reasons to use other truncations -- for example,
for data with a long, flat tail and a short spike in detections close to 0
then more severe truncation can sometimes yield a more reliable result.
Other examples of different truncations are given in the book.

If you want to use the g(y) approx 0.15 suggestion (which is a good one)
then remember that the value where g(y)=0.15 will change depending on the
model you fit, so you're really only looking to find that value very
approximately.  Probably the best way to do this is to read it off the
detection function plot that Distance provides!  In your case, g(27) is
0.1459, so it appears using this function that 5% truncation also gives you
g(y) approx. 0.15.

If you really do want to find the exact value, the following R code will do
it.  The result is y=26.81.

Cheers,

 - Len

-------------------------------------------
#R code (www.r-project.org <http://www.r-project.org>) to find
#g(y)=0.15 for Jennifer's detection funcion

g<-function(y) {
#Returns g(y) given y
  unscaled<-function(y) {
    return(exp (-y^2/(2*13.76^2)) *(1+0.1651*cos(2*pi*y/27)) )
  }
  scaled<-unscaled(y)/unscaled(0)
  return(scaled)

sq.diff<-function(y) {
#returns squared difference between
#g(y) and 0.15
  return((g(y)-0.15)^2)

#find value for which sq.diff is minimized --
# ie for which g(y) is closest to 0.15
ret<-optimize(sq.diff,c(0,27))

#output result
cat("g(y)=.15 at y=",ret$minimum,"\n")
-------------------------------------------

--

messages.body_plain:
Steve Buckland kindly pointed out an over-simplification I made in the

previous message when I said:

> >Answer: In the case of the cosine series, j is the order of the adjustment
> >term.  The default method in Distance is to start with an adjustment of
> >order 2, and if that gives lower AIC to try order 3 as well, then order 4,
> >etc.  For simple and hermite polynomial series, j is the order/2, since it
> >doesn't make sense to have odd ordered terms.  The default in Distance for
> >these series is to start with an adjustment of order 4, then try 6, 8 etc.

Actually, this is only correct for the half-normal and hazard rate keys.
For the uniform key, the default is to start with order 1 for cosine series
and order 2 for the polynomial series.  If you're interested, try plotting
the shape of the series and you'll soon see why.

The appropriate formulae and starting orders are all given in the table at
the top of page 47 of the 2001 book , or starting at the bootom of page 46
of the 1993 book.

I don't know what the default is for the negative exponential key as I never
use it!  ;-)

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: Why can't the Design tab in the project browser not always be
messages.subject_clean: Why can't the Design tab in the project browser not always be
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martijn,

The design tab is only activated when the project is geographic -- ie it
contains geographic information.  This is because the automated survey design
algorithms require explicit geographic data (the location of the corners of
your study area, etc) entered (or imported) into the built-in GIS.

The best way to set up a project for survey design is to follow the
instructions on the last page of Chapter 6 of the online manual.

However, you can convert a non-geographic project (such as D4Ducknest) to a
geographic one if you want to.  Open the project, then click on File | Project
Properties, then on the Geographic tab, and tick the box "Project can contain
geographic information".  Set the appropriate projects (or none if none), and
click OK.  This now means the project *can* contain geographic information,
but it doesn't contain any yet.  (E.g., if you look under the layer properties
for any data layer, you'll see it has no geographic data.)  Geographic data is
stored in ESRI shapefile format, and there's no way to add these to the
existing layers using the Distance interface.  Instead, you'd need to delete
all the data layers already there and re-create them with associated
shapefiles.  Alternatively, shapefiles can be linked in to existing data
layers by mucking around with the Data File (the .mdb in the data folder - see
Appendix - Inside Distance) -- but I wouldn't recommend this for most people.

Hope this helps, and sorry if the manual is unclear,

 - Len

--

Below are the results from the runs in the attached document:

Please let me know
Thanks
Murray

messages.subject: Re: Probability of a Greater Chi-Square Value vs Chi-p
messages.subject_clean: Probability of a Greater Chi-Square Value vs Chi-p
messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray, list,

Firstly, you can't send attachments to the list, which is why yours didn't
appear.  This is to prevent viruses being spread by the list.

Nevertheless, it's still possible to make a good guess at the answer to your
question.  Distance often does several chi-sq tests on the same set of data,
and the one it reports in the summary page is the last test it did.

Why does it do more than one test?

- Firstly, if you don't specify your own cutpoints for exact data, Distance
produces 3 plots and 3 sets of chi-sq tests, with a small, medium and large
number of intervals.  (The exact rule for choosing number of intervals is n^
0.5, 2/3n^0.5 and 3/2n^0.5 where n is the number of observations.)

- Secondly, the method of calculating a chi-sq value is known to give a poor
approximation of the chi-sq distribution when the expected cell counts are
small (see any stats book).  So, if any of the intervals has an expected
value less than 2, Distance will do a second test where it pools adjacent
intervals until all intervals have values greater than 2.  It starts pooling
from the 1st interval downwards (only useful for point transect data, where
the expected count in the first interval can be small), and from the last
interval upwards.  These pooled intervals are then used to perform a second
test, which is shown after the first one in the Chi-sq GOF test page of
results.

Note that, for exact data, Distance now provides Kolmogorov-Smirnov and
Craemer-von Mises tests.  These are better as they avoid the need to pool
the data.  Other things being equal, the uniform weighting CvM test should
be more powerful to detect departures from the fitted model than the KS
test, so that's the one I'd quote.  The cosine weighting CvM should be
better at detecting departures close to 0 distance (see online help for more
on this) - but we haven't evaluated it by simulation yet, and I've found the
two to give very similar results.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: spatial distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Stefano, we hope to have the simple count method in Distance within the
next year.  More sophisticated methods, including methods that model
autocorrelation, are a bit further down the line, but should be in
Distance in under 3 years.  Meantime:

> > In wish to perform a spatial distance sampling analysis in order to

> > develop a spatially explicit map for density in a roe deer population of

> > conservation interest. The aim is to identify  high density areas where

> > to adopt "expensive" conservation measures.
> >
> > During the last years a number of classical distance sampling surveys

> > were made through the study area, trying to estimate population size but

> > where the exact location of the animals was also recorded
> >
> > I've studied cap 4 of "Advanced distance sampling" book for spatial

> > line transects method,  but before developing a procedure in SAS to do
> > the job I'd like to be sure about some points which I've not well

> > understood.
> >
> > all OK until eq 4.4 . I've not understood what f((u1....) is.

This is the probability density function of detection locations (u,v),
evaluated at each location that you detected an animal, and the product
taken across the detected animals.

> > section 4.3
> >
> > the GAM has to be fitted to spatial covariates z. I presume that in the

> > most simple case one should use the x coordinates, or both the x and y

> > coordinates?

Yes, in the simplest case, z would probably be x and y.  The x and y
distances would then be proxies for whatever it is that causes variation
in animal density within your survey region.

> > pag 56. is mu_hat  the effective strip width estimated from CDS on the

> > whole study area?

Yes.  We're working on methods to integrate estimation of mu with the
spatial modelling, but we're not there yet.

> > it is not clear to me how to adjust the waiting distance l . I do not

> > understand the difference between D_hat (x,0) and D_hat (xi,0).

> >
> >  I presume that D_hat (xi,0) is the average density estimated by CDS

> > but what I missed what really means  D_hat (xi,0)is the value obtained
> > from eq.
> >
> > (2mu_hat l)^-1

Having fitted the density surface D^(x,y), then D^(x_i,0) is the value of
this function at x=x_i (the x value of detection i) and y=0.  D^(x,0) is
still this function evaluated at y=0, but now with no value substituted in
for x.  Hence the 2-dimensional surface is now a one-dimensional function,
which we integrate between x=x_{i-1} and x=x_i.

> > I imagine that what I'd do is to compute the mean density for the whole

> > study area using the values estimated for each segment and "oblige" the

> > program to set that CDS density and spatial DS density be the same over

> > the whole study area.

That is not what we intend, as the spatial method can give you a more
precise estimate of overall density.  If you rescale it to match the CDS
estimate, you will lose the extra precision.

> > Finally, what can be a good criterion to establish that iteration has

> > converged? Maybe that

> >
> > absolute value (mean of D_hat (xi,0) - CDS density) <0.0001?

It depends on the units you're using to estimate density, but it converges
quickly, so any small value is likely to work well.  One possibility might
be that l'_i in one iteration differs from the previous iteration by less
than 0.0001*l'_i for each i.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Free distance sampling books
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance list:

The publisher of "Introduction to Distance Sampling", Oxford University Press,
have discovered that a batch of the books have been printed incorrectly, with
pages 305-336 inserted between pages 272 and 273.  All the pages are there,
just in the wrong order.  The publisher say they have a policy of sending
faulty books to charititable organizations where possible, so if any of you
can think of a worthy recipient please contact our admin person: Rhona Rodger
(rh...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk).  I'm not sure how many books they're talking about,
and the recipient will probably have to pay shipping.

Cheers,

 - Len
